1:
Gill takes the opening formula to mark a fresh prophecy rather than a continuation, of the same kind as the one before it but distinct from it, and notes that the Targum calls it the word of prophecy from the Lord. Calvin presses the same point harder, because he feels the objection: the prophet seems here too verbose, repeating the same sentiments in almost the same words. His answer is that a people slow to believe and perverse in disposition would have found a short command cold and ineffectual. The prophet was not sent once but often, and the repetition was itself the instrument. Had everything been gathered into one discourse, Calvin argues, the Israelites might have thought of the judgment for a moment, but a prophecy once uttered would easily have escaped them.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the architecture. This second word completes the announcement of judgment upon Jerusalem and Judah by expanding the thought that the end will come both quickly and inevitably. It divides into two unequal sections marked by the repeated formula: the first states the theme in short, monotonous clauses, and the second is arranged in four strophes, resembling in form a lamentation. Clarke gives the same map in different terms, tracing the destruction of the land, the distress of the small remnant that escapes, the devoting of the polluted temple, and the chain that typifies the captivity of both king and people to Babylon. He adds that the whole chapter abounds in bold and beautiful figures, and is poetry throughout.

On the doubled announcement the voices converge. Ellicott calls it repetition for the sake of emphasis, and observes that the frequent repetitions of this chapter are designed and give great force to the denunciation. Clarke goes to the manuscripts: against the received text he prefers a reading found in copies collated by Kennicott and De Rossi and in one of his own, supported by all the ancient versions, which yields the end cometh, come is the end. He notes that the pointing of his oldest copy was added by a later hand which quietly cancelled a word to make the text square with the received tradition, though the original reading is still discernible. Wesley reduces the whole to a sentence: an end of God patience, and of the peace and welfare of the people.

The four corners draw a further note. Ellicott denies that the phrase rests on any popular belief that the earth was square, deriving it instead from the fact that so many common things had four sides, so that it came naturally to express universality. Calvin reads it as a rebuke of obstinacy: God had hitherto chastised moderately, and whenever the hand was withdrawn the people thought themselves escaped and went on so carelessly that they plainly despised him. After this, he says, they must hope for no moderation. Henry hears a town crier rather than an orator, a man who does not seek fine words but cries fire in the streets, and warns that though the ruin of sinners comes slowly it comes surely.

Gill narrows the address: the mountains and valleys were spoken to before, but now the land itself, and not the ten tribes already carried away, but Judah and Benjamin and those still dwelling there. Henry dwells on the evil called an only evil, an evil that stands alone and has no precedent, needing no second stroke to finish its work; yet he adds that the same affliction is a half evil or an only evil according as men conduct themselves under it, since some were sent to Babylon for their good. To the impenitent it only hardens the heart, and for them the time of reckoning is fixed whether they see it or not.
3:
Calvin counts the repetitions: the word is put a third time, and repeated a fourth and a fifth. Those miserable ones, admonished more than enough by teaching and experience, were still like brute animals, always promising themselves something to fly to. They did not think an end was really coming, but said that some would escape, and this was their pride. Gill reads the shift from the third person to the second as a device to arouse a people who would not attend. Calvin adds that the past judgments were partial, God having given them time for repentance had they been curable, so that the burden now cast on them is their own.

On the divine pity Calvin is severe. When hypocrites hear that God is merciful they seize on it and fabricate a foolish confidence, not knowing why he testifies this of himself, which is that sinners may fearlessly call upon him. Mercy is not accessible to those who do not cease to repel it. Clarke turns the verse outward: the abominations set in the midst will stare them in the face and stand as witnesses against them.

The cry of an evil, an only evil, divides the voices, and the division is textual. Ellicott glosses the received reading as an evil so all-embracing as to be complete in itself and to need no repetition, comparing the promise that affliction shall not rise up a second time; but he notes that some copies and the Chaldee, by altering one letter, read evil after evil. Clarke reports the variant and prefers it, so that one evil instantly succeeds another. Calvin thinks the sense the same either way and argues for the succession: there will be no cessation in the heaping of evils until the name of the people is extinct. He calls the alternative subtle and unsatisfactory. Wesley keeps to a singular, uncommon affliction, and elsewhere adds that temporal judgments have their allays while the torments of the damned are an evil, an only evil.

Clarke finds a play on words in the doubled end, joining the root that means to cut off with the one that means to awake from sleep, and with the noun for summer, when the earth seems to wake from winter. So the end is personified as an executioner risen early, waiting for orders. The word rendered morning is rarer still. Ellicott observes that it is not the usual term and occurs elsewhere only twice, once translated crown, and proposes circuit, so that the circuit of their sins is finished. Gill reports the reading that makes it a crowned head, the king of Babylon, following the Targum. Calvin rejects that as distorted language. On the sounding again of the mountains, Ellicott hears the joyous harvest cries echoing back from the hills, now replaced by the trouble of the day of war; Clarke hears advancing troops and tells them not to mistake the tumult for festivity; Calvin denies it is an echo at all, since every one shall cry out in earnest. Gill dates the whole from the sixth year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, about three years before Nebuchadnezzar came up against Jerusalem, which is why the fury is called near.

Calvin makes the morning a figure of exposure. Hypocrites sin as if no eye were upon them and think to enjoy perpetual night; as the rising day dispels darkness, so the judgment appears suddenly and too late. The time named is fixed beforehand, which takes from them the material of their pride. Ellicott notes that the closing formula is here made more precise than in the earlier refrain: they will know not merely that he is the Lord, but that he is the Lord that smiteth. Calvin says the same, that this is how God makes himself known to the reprobate, who are compelled to feel what they would not believe.
10:
The central question of this passage is who the rod is, and the voices split. Gill reports that some understand it of the Chaldeans, a rod in the hand of the Lord to scourge the Jews, and says the Targum seems to read it so. Calvin thinks it not doubtful that the rod means Nebuchadnezzar, but immediately notes that interpreters vary over what follows: many refer the next clause to the king of Babylon, while others, in his judgment rightly, take it of the Israelites themselves. Pride here is not simple haughtiness but the licentiousness that springs from contempt of God, which does not suit the Babylonians, whom God was governing with his own hand. So the staff grew in Chaldea while the root was at home. Ellicott presses further and makes the rod itself domestic. The word for rod is also the word for tribe, and he takes it as a play: where the rod of Aaron budded by divine power in evidence of his choosing, the rod standing for the tribe at Jerusalem has budded to its own destruction. Violence, he insists, has risen up not into a rod for punishing wickedness but into a wicked people.

Keil and Delitzsch give the strophe its heading in a sentence: the rod is already prepared, and nothing will be left of the ungodly. The three clauses are synonymous but rise in force, the fate springing up out of the earth. Calvin turns the image into an argument about delay. God plants as a husbandman plants, waiting until the tree rises to a just magnitude; he could destroy without human help, since all creatures are at hand to fulfil his commands, but he provides ministers of vengeance and lets them reach maturity. If he does not hasten as we wish, the rods are still prepared and only the appointed time is wanting. Clarke reads the repetitions as alarm rather than architecture: the morning will wait no longer, the rod is quite ready, and their insolence and daring opposition have brought forth their proper fruits.

Clarke finds the next verse genuinely obscure. The ideas succeed each other so rapidly that the prophet cannot find language for each, leaving broken sentences; Houbigant, who rarely admits himself puzzled, is completely nonplussed, and Calmet offers five interpretations. Clarke settles for the plainest sense: neither their multitude nor their struggles will free them, and their desolation will be so deserved that none shall lament them. Ellicott notes that the word rendered wailing occurs only here and is now generally taken to mean what is glorious, so that of their glory nothing shall be left. Calvin reports that Jerome rendered it rest, and explains the absence of mourning by scale: when one family perishes friends assemble and celebrate the funeral, but when a pestilence pervades a whole city and fathers lie mingled with sons, all sorrow ceases.

On the buyer and the seller, Clarke is practical. The man forced by want to sell need not mourn, since the enemy would soon have taken it; the buyer need not rejoice, since he will be stripped of his purchase. Wesley adds that men grieve to transmit their right to others, and should now consider how little a while either party will keep the land. Calvin marks off a distinction here that he thinks is often blurred. Paul exhorts the pious to pass through the world as pilgrims, since its fashion passes away, a general doctrine for the children of God, who possess what is conferred on them as though not possessing. But the prophet means something else: not a lesson in detachment but a ruin so complete that neither money nor lands will have any use, since all will be cast out of their country and reduced to want.
13:
The law of jubilee governs this passage and every voice reaches for it. Gill explains that a man who had sold his possession returned to it in the fiftieth year, whether the sale had stood thirty years or ten; and since the captivity was to run seventy years, a jubilee must fall within it, yet those who had sold would be captives in another land and could not come back. Clarke says the same and adds the further difficulty that the seller was not likely to be alive when the next jubilee came, and would not possess the land even if he were. Ellicott sets the point against the previous verse: buying and selling land was the chief business among the Israelites, the law forbade any sale reaching past the jubilee, and the desolation is now to last so long that the year of release will be useless. He quotes Jerome to close it off, that it is natural to rejoice in a purchase and mourn over a sale, but when slavery and captivity stare a man in the face, rejoicing and mourning are equally absurd.

Calvin adds a reconciliation the others do not attempt. If the sellers are told they will never return, what of the command to buy a field from a kinsman while in prison? He answers that the purchase was made so that the faithful might wait for the promised restitution with quiet minds, whereas this discourse is aimed at the reprobate, shut out from all hope of freedom; the prophet breathes nothing but terror, and no favour is mentioned because they had cast themselves into despair. He reads the clause about their life adversatively: though they live among the living, even to a hundred years, their possession will lie deserted, because the conquerors will not let them return.

Over the clause that the vision shall not return Calvin records a disagreement and declines the more attractive side of it. Some divide it into two thoughts, so that the vision went out to the whole people and yet no one repented, which he grants is plausible and holds a fruitful doctrine met everywhere in the prophets, since nothing is less tolerable to God than men who are admonished and go on in their wickedness. He nevertheless does not adopt it. He takes the sense to be that the prophecy shall not be in vain, comparing the word that does not return void, because prophecies are always joined with their effects.

The trumpet draws a small textual note and a large irony. Gill records a reading followed by the Septuagint and the Arabic version that makes it a command to blow, which he would take as sarcasm: sound the alarm, and see what comes of it. On the other reading the Jews blew to gather the towns into a posture of defence. Clarke calls all such efforts vain, since the people will be dispirited and none will go to the battle; Wesley says flatly that the house of Israel summoned all fit for arms and not a man went to the war, the wrath itself taking away their courage. Ellicott traces the failure to the sins that have enfeebled them.

At the last verse the escape routes close. Gill sets the enemy outside the city, so that those who went out to escape fell into his hands. Clarke divides country from city, war through the one and pestilence and famine within the other, and says the man who flees the one falls by the other. Calvin makes the point about reach rather than geography: God could fetch destruction from various quarters, arming foreign enemies to devastate the land, and if those were at rest there were others still, so that though the Israelites shut their houses against every injurious thing, his wrath could penetrate all their hiding places.
16:
Escape here is not mercy, and the voices labour to show why. Gill says only a few get past the pestilence, the famine and the sword, fleeing to the mountains to live a miserable life, so the wrath pronounced on the whole multitude is not contradicted. Calvin admits the difficulty more openly: the prophet seems at variance with himself, having devoted all to destruction and now sending some to hiding places. The two agree, he answers, because the life of those who escaped was worse than death by sword or plague. By mountains he understands dry and desert places, where a man hides anxious only to preserve a life he does not expect to keep. Nor will they dare cry out; and since the last solace in evils is that men complain freely and unburden themselves by weeping, the wretch who dares not complain is twice dead among the living.

Henry works the same thought through a longer picture. They escape only as Cain did, fugitives and vagabonds afraid of being slain by everyone they meet, carrying guilty consciences that make them a burden to themselves. They keep away from cities and places of concourse, not loving solitude but ashamed of what they have come to. Those who once thought themselves lions of the mountains have become doves of the valleys, fleeing when none pursues and trembling at the shaking of a leaf. He is careful about the mourning: it is not godly sorrow but the sorrow of the world which works death, and its subject is not only the guilt of the land but each man own share in it. Sooner or later, he adds, sin will have sorrow of one kind or another, and those who will not mourn for it as an offence against God will mourn for it as their own ruin.

The dove image is read two ways. Clarke prefers mourning doves, chased from their cotes and separated from their mates. Ellicott keeps the valleys as the birds proper home, from which fear has driven them into the mountains, and says their mourning belongs to exile. On the phrase every one for his iniquity he is flat: iniquity means the punishment of iniquity, and repentance is not brought forward at all. Wesley leaves both doors open, saying it is either the punishment of their iniquity or the iniquity itself.

The failing hands and watery knees are taken bodily. Gill leaves them no strength to lift a weapon and no courage to meet the enemy, afraid even to raise their voice in mourning lest they be heard and pursued. Calvin makes it a doctrine about who holds the heart: profane men are fierce against God through trust in their wealth or fortitude, and against that God pronounces them timorous and almost lifeless, their knees flowing away like water. Clarke reports that Calmet and Jerome explained the weakness quite literally, as the loss of bodily control that terror brings on, and believes them nearly right, such failures being natural effects of extreme fear.

Calvin meets one more apparent contradiction at the sackcloth. If they are too astonished to bewail their dead, how do they gird themselves for mourning? He answers that the prophet describes not what they will do but what the event will be, the prophets varying their speech because obstinate minds cannot otherwise be reached. He then refuses to read the signs as penitence. Sackcloth is a known symbol of repentance but is often transferred to common grief, and profane men wear it without acknowledging who sent the evil; baldness the law had forbidden outright, God restraining an ambitious intemperance in sorrow. So they cut themselves after the manner of the Gentiles and put on sackcloth like men abandoned to destruction. Wesley notes only that the baldness came by pulling the hair out in grief or cutting it off as a token.
19:
Calvin makes the silver thrown into the street a measure of despair: men are more anxious about such possessions than about life itself, so that when they despise gold they must have lost their senses through fear. Had they thought they would survive, they would have hidden it. Ellicott takes the image from the field, where a routed soldier throws away his most valuable things as impediments to flight and temptations to the pursuer. Wesley agrees on the motive, that they may be the lighter to fly. Clarke puts it bluntly: a pound of gold is not worth an ounce of bread. Gill adds a reading from Kimchi, that the silver and gold may be their idols of the same metals, now cast away in contempt for failing to save.

Over the strong word applied to the gold there is a small difference. Ellicott says the original is harsher than the English, making their gold an unclean thing, filth, because they perceive it has been an occasion of sin. Calvin knows the same range, pollution, defilement and separation, and prefers a casting away as answering the first half of the sentence better. On the stumbling block Calvin chooses the narrower of two options: some take it generally, that the Jews stumble on account of their iniquity, but he restricts it to the money itself as the occasion of sinning. Wesley reads a reversal: what they stumbled at and fell into sin by, they now stumble at and fall into misery by.

The next verse divides the field for the rest of the passage. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all take the beauty of the ornament to be the temple. Gill gives the alternative first, that the gifts were turned to pride instead of supporting worship and the poor, but says the temple is rather meant, following Jarchi and Kimchi. Clarke agrees, adding that they took its riches to make idols and brought them into the very courts. Ellicott refuses the temple entirely: what was given for the beauty of ornament is the silver and gold of the previous verse, perverted to pride and then made into idols, every pronoun in the verse referring to the people. Calvin refuses it too, on the ground that the prophet explains himself by naming gold and silver. He grants that the temple was the chief glory of the Jews, but will not read it here. He sets out instead the lawful use of wealth, since whatever God gives testifies to paternal favour as health and honours do, and names two profanations: pride, when abundance made them insolent, and idolatry, when they made their gods out of the gift, as another prophet complains that the corn and wine and oil he gave were spent on idols.

Calvin keeps the same line at the plundering. The strangers are remote and barbarous nations, the more savage for having no communication with the victims, and no pity is to be looked for. From this he draws a general rule, that abandoned men are the scourges of God, governed by his hand, yet he is pure from all alliance with their faults, since their own avarice and ambition condemn them. On the word rendered pollute he notes it can mean to slay, giving a slaughter of the captives, but keeps profane in the sense of rendering vile. At the last verse he parts from the expositors again: they take the secret place as the holy of holies, and he does not greatly object, but prefers the land itself as an asylum under the wings of God, so that every bulwark falls at once. Ellicott holds to the shrine, guarded from all intrusion and the summit of the national life, and names the robbers as the invading armies. Wesley takes it both ways, and reads the face turned away as a double abandonment, relieving neither the Jews nor restraining their enemies.
23:
The chain is read two ways, and the difference is between a prison and a courtroom. Gill offers both, to bring them to the bar or to lead them bound into captivity, and notes that it binds the Jews, not the Chaldeans. Clarke and Wesley keep the plainer sense of captivity. Ellicott observes that in an unfigured prophecy the prophet mind still runs to the symbolic act, though here it can only be done in word. Calvin sets himself against the majority. Interpreters refer it to exile because captives are bound with fetters, but he thinks the allusion is to criminals who plead their cause in chains, already as it were half condemned. The Jews had long revelled in their vices and impunity had made them audacious; now they are drawn, whether they wish it or not, to the judgment seat.

Henry works the passage as a trial. The prisoner is arraigned, dragged to the bar in fetters like a notorious malefactor, and those who break the bands of the law asunder find themselves held by chains of judgment they cannot cast off. Then the indictment: the land is full of the judgments of blood, which he takes as guilt incurred under colour of justice and with the solemnity of a legal sentence, the innocent blood Manasseh shed being the sin that filled the measure. Calvin glosses it as any capital conviction, where the criminal cannot escape, and notes that the charge is not only against worship: the city is charged with violence, a word gathering up oppression, rapine, unlawful gain and everything against equity. Henry adds that the rulers, having the greater power, were the greater oppressors, and asks how the faithful city has become a harlot.

On the worst of the heathen the voices part again. Gill and Clarke take worst morally, of the Chaldeans as the most cruel and idolatrous of nations. Ellicott takes it of capacity rather than character, of the power and thoroughness of their work, pointing back to the ancient warnings in the law where the word now rendered pomp of the strong was translated pride of power. Henry holds both together: some of the heathen are worse than others, and God picks out the worst to scourge his own people, intending them for the fire when the work is done. Calvin adds his usual caution, that the impious cannot move a finger but by God will, and yet he has nothing in common with them, since they are carried by a depraved impulse.

The defiling of the holy places confirms Calvin earlier reading, since the prophet takes away the hope by which the people boasted of a guardianship the temple secured. Another prophet had reproved them for trusting in lying words while repeating that they had the temple of the Lord. God dwelt there on condition of pure worship, and when the place was polluted he departed. Ellicott makes the point in a phrase, that they are called their holy places and no longer his, because he has abandoned them for the sin of the people. Wesley allows the pomp to be their magnificence or the temple itself. Henry adds the symmetry: they defiled the holy places with idolatry, so God defiles them with judgments, and places deserted by their God are soon defiled by their enemies.

At the last verse Ellicott notes another word peculiar to this chapter, generally explained of the dismay that accompanies great judgments. Clarke supplies the history, that their ceasing to pay tribute to the king of Babylon had brought the Chaldeans on them, and they sue for peace in vain. Calvin explains why the denial had to be said at all: men hope to gain by turning their backs, seizing hiding places out of which God draws them into the light, so that being slippery they are told plainly they shall seek peace and find none.
26:
Gill reads the piling of mischief on mischief as one calamity treading on another, as in the case of Job. Calvin explains why a heap is described rather than a single blow: the wicked, once God withdraws his hand, think themselves clear of trouble, like a debtor who has paid a small sum, gained a relaxation and grown careless, imagining an agreement that he will trouble them no more. So even the rumours are part of the punishment, one calamity being the forerunner of another.

Ellicott names the structure of what follows. The three chief sources of guidance, the prophets, the priests and the elders, are applied to in vain, because God has forsaken a people who first rejected him; he compares the despair of Saul at finding himself abandoned. Clarke makes it a general observation about the eve of national judgments: God restrains the influences of his Spirit, his word goes without its usual unction, and the celebrated statesmen of the land devise foolish schemes, hastening the ruin they meant to avert. He quotes the old saying that those whom God designs to destroy he first infatuates. Wesley keeps it short: they seek in vain, the priest having no word of counsel and the senators no advice.

Calvin finds the clause about seeking a vision awkwardly compressed, since nothing is added except concerning the priest and the elders, and he wonders whether a particle should be read negatively, so that the prophet denies there will be any prophets at all. He admits the language may not bear it, though the sense would flow better, and notes that the Church elsewhere complains that no prophet is among them. Either way they thought God so bound to them that he would never take away the visions prepared for their comfort. He then makes this the heaviest of the threats. In extreme evils it is no common consolation to have God shining on us by his word; while his teaching remains we have a chart of guidance that brings us into harbour, but when he nowhere appears the lightest trial buries us in the deepest abyss.

The last verse spreads the judgment across the ranks, and the voices differ over who is meant. Gill takes king and prince as one and the same, naming Zedekiah, who saw his children killed before him, then lost his eyes and was carried in chains to Babylon. Wesley agrees on the king but takes the prince of every magistrate. Calvin reads three ranks rather than two, the king, his counsellors and the whole people, and notes what a mourning king implies: it is his office to give life to others and devise a remedy for every evil, so that when nothing is left him but grief it is a sign of despair. On the elders he presses the clothing metaphor: a garment defends against cold and hides what is dishonourable, and here the covering given them is shame itself.

Calvin also flags a word used against its ordinary sense at the close. Judgment commonly means righteousness, but is often transferred to transgressions, so that what is repaid is their perverse abuses, taking in not only superstitions but every kind of iniquity; by which God signifies that however severely he punishes it will not be cruelty. Wesley asks what men can contrive for themselves when God is departed from them. Ellicott closes the whole series here rather than the verse. This is the end of the first group of prophecies, running from the fourth chapter to this one within a year and two months. The exiles had been five or six years away, still looking to Jerusalem and the temple as the strength of the nation and many hoping to return to their former lives; and there could be no lasting reformation except by dashing those hopes to the ground, which is what these chapters were for.
